catalog_citation: Chumbow, Beban Sammy. 1982. Contraction and tone polarization in Ogori. Journal of West African Languages 12(1): 89-103.
catalog_locator: p. 99 (PDF page 11 of 14;, page image the page image, scanned); Tone Reduction Principle pp. 100-101
catalog_quote: The process of creation and subsequent reduction of tonal glides and duplex tones differs from corresponding processes at the segmental level in that the tonemes undergo neither ASSIMILATION nor ELISION as their corresponding segments. This supports a suprasegmental analysis of tone to capture the fact that tone is immune to the assimilation and elision processes at the segmental level. ... There are four possible ways of accounting for the behaviour of tone in these paradigms. Three of these involve assuming that the adjective or pronoun has one of the three Ogori tones as its underlying tone (low, mid, high).
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

new_statements.rule_in_words: Ogori/Òkó is described as a tone language with three level tonemes (low, mid, high) plus derived tonal glides and duplex tones that reduce by the hierarchy H > L > M; no source opened says anything about word stress or accent. Corroborated second-hand by Storch's 2013 review of Atoyebi 2010, which reports 'die drei Tonemen des Oko (hoch, mittel, tief)' and that vowel length is not significant, and by the TOC of Atoyebi 2010 whose only suprasegmental section is §3.5 'The Òko tone system'.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed in any opened source.
new_statements.exceptions: None relevant to stress; Chumbow notes tonal glides surface only in deliberate (slow) speech and are reduced in normal speech.
new_statements.domain_note: Chumbow's data are cross-word-boundary (noun+adjective, possessive+noun, pronoun+verb) contraction phenomena; the three-tone statement concerns the lexical tone inventory. Nothing on citation-form vs phrase-level prominence.
new_statements.identity_note: Chumbow 1982 and the Ilorin theses use the name 'Ogori' (the town / Oko dialect); Atoyebi 2010 treats Oko (Ogori) and Osanyen (Magongo) as two dialects with minor phonological differences and rejects Eni as a distinct dialect; Akerejola writes Ò̩kọ/Òkó. All refer to the Oko dialect of okoe1238; no separate glottocode needed.
